quotes.text: Santana's musical journey, as presented through previously unseen material from the artist's personal archives including photos, drawings, posters, and mementos, reveals the deliberate curation of a creative legacy.

In retrospect, "Smooth," accidentally or not, rode a few different waves. The song came on the heels of the Latin pop explosion, the manufactured and hyped-up blast of excitement that still made full-on mainstream stars out of figures like Ricky Martin, Jennifer Lopez, and Enrique Iglesias. The song also took advantage of the burst in growly post-grunge soft rock that had put "Smooth" singer and co-writer Rob Thomas' band Matchbox 20 on top.
"Smooth" stacks hooks on top of hooks, and those hooks are the diamond-sharp type that sink into your brain, that can never be extracted.

"Smooth" wasn't a random occurrence that took everyone by storm. Instead, it's the best-case scenario for record-label meddling, the kind of thing that every A&R rep envisions when they give notes about how an album really needs a single. The people who made "Smooth" all deliberately set out to craft a hit, and they all succeeded to a degree that they couldn't possibly have imagined.
When he made "Smooth," Carlos Santana wasn't a contemporary hitmaker, but he was a familiar name. The man wasn't starting from zero. He'd already done that.

In some ways, the pan-racial and stylistically omnivorous Santana fit right into a psych-rock zeitgeist that also included bands like fellow Woodstock standouts Sly & The Family Stone. In other ways, though, Santana were a true anomaly. The band played blistering blues-rock, but they also went heavy on percussion, bringing in sounds and rhythms from different forms of Latin music.
A boomer icon, famous for virtuosity and for genre-blurring hybridism, had captured the mass imagination in a time when teen pop was on the rise.
He paved a path unknown, a skilled guitarist honoring his Mexican roots by fusing timbales and congas with melodic, blues-based lines.

After moving to San Francisco in the early 1960s, he became intoxicated by the city's psychedelic rock scene, merging it with the Latin rhythms, blues, and jazz of his roots. This melting pot of influences was never explored before, but Carlos knew there was something pounding in him to be born.

Together, they played music that felt near ancestral, celebrating their united Latin identity through a spiritual and revolutionary sound. It was important to Carlos that there always be divine meaning embedded within their catalog, a through line that followed until the end.
Santana's music became increasingly introspective and spiritually influenced, particularly after Carlos' connection with the Indian guru Sri Chinmoy in the 1970s.
Their percussion-driven performance felt like a psychedelic thrill ride, immediately winning over the audience of half a million help captive.
The hypnotic blend of congas, timbales, electric guitar, and soulful vocals was incomparable to anything else in the industry, a nearly complete instrumental recorded as a free-form jam.

It was after the release of Santana that the term "Latin rock" was born, an attempt to define this unexplored musical landscape. What was unbeknownst to them then was that this would go on to birth an entire genre, giving permission for Latin artists to explore new territory and express themselves with limitless capabilities.
His impact not only reshaped the way artists related to their instruments, but it also disintegrated cultural boundaries, paving the way for Latin fusion across genres.
